Question 11. PhD CS 1405, Q21 — Minimum count outside three sets

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 8 · question 21. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

Thirty-two offices each have a computer. Fifteen have a laser printer, ten have a scanner, eight have a modem, and two have all three. What is the minimum number with none of these three devices?

1.

1

2.

2

3.

3

4.

4

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

  1. The membership total is 15+10+8=33. The two triple members contribute six memberships but only two union elements, so they force four duplicated memberships.
  2. Consequently the union has at most 33-4=29 members. Additional pair-only overlaps would make it smaller.
  3. The upper bound is attainable: use two triple offices, thirteen printer-only offices, eight scanner-only offices, and six modem-only offices. This uses 29 offices and has no pair-only overlaps.
  4. Exactly three of the 32 offices are outside this maximal union. One and two violate the forced duplication; four is possible but is not the minimum.

Transfer rule. Optimize a union under forced overlaps and prove the bound is attainable.

Question 12. PhD CS 1404, Q68 — At most one independent event

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 15 · question 68. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

Events B1,…,Bn are independent, and P(Bi)=1/n. What is the probability that at most one occurs? Take n≥2 in the displayed formulas.

1.
(n-1)n-1(2n-1)nn
2.
nn-1(2n-1)(n+1)n
3.
(n/(n-1))n
4.
((n-1)/(n+1))n
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

  1. No event occurs with probability (1-1/n)n by mutual independence.
  2. Exactly one occurs in n disjoint ways, each of probability (1/n)(1-1/n)n-1. Their total is (1-1/n)n-1.
  3. Add the two cases and factor:
(1-1/n)n-1(2-1/n)=(n-1)n-1(2n-1)/nn

. 4. The other options use a different success probability or omit the exactly-one contribution. For n=2 the correct result is 3/4, a quick check against alternatives.

Transfer rule. At most one includes zero; pairwise independence alone would not justify multiplying all complements.

Question 13. PhD CS 1404, Q70 — Equal heads from unequal sample sizes

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 16 · question 70. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

Player A tosses a fair coin 25 times and player B tosses a fair coin 20 times, independently. What is the probability that they obtain the same number of heads?

1.
(4520)2-45
2.
(4515)2-45
3.
(4520)2-20
4.
(4515)2-20
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

  1. Sum over their common head count k:
P=2-45∑k=020(25k)(20k)

. 2. Replace (20k) by (2020-k) and apply Vandermonde's identity. The sum is (4520). 3. Alternatively, equal heads means the heads in A's tosses plus the tails in B's tosses total 20. Those 45 independent fair indicators give the same binomial coefficient. 4. The denominator counts all 45 tosses; 220 is insufficient. The index 15 represents the wrong combined target.

Transfer rule. Convert equality between two counts into one count by complementing one group's successes.

Question 14. PhD CS 1404, Q25 — A subset containing an odd pair sum

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 7 · question 25. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

How many four-element subsets A of {1,2,…,10} contain two elements x,y such that x+y is odd?

1.

200

2.

205

3.

208

4.

209

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

  1. A sum is odd exactly when one summand is even and the other odd. Thus the set must contain both parities.
  2. There are (104)=210 unrestricted subsets. The failing subsets consist entirely of the five even or entirely of the five odd elements.
  3. Subtract 2(54)=10 to get 200. The two failure classes are disjoint, so no overlap correction is required.
  4. Counting a chosen odd/even pair and then two other elements would overcount sets containing several witness pairs.

Transfer rule. Count an existential-witness property by its complement when each valid object may have several witnesses.

Concept model supporting this solution

Question 15. MSc CE 1405, Q35 — Heads in a conditional second toss

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 8 · question 35. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

Four fair coins are tossed. Every coin that showed heads is tossed again. If Y is the number of heads in the second toss, what is P(Y=2)?

1.
1/2
2.
3/4
3.
17/128
4.
27/128
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 4.

  1. Model each coin by two independent fair tosses, with the second revealed only when the first is heads. A coin contributes one to Y exactly on the outcome heads-heads, which has probability 1/4.
  2. The four contribution indicators are independent, so Y is binomial with parameters 4 and 1/4. Exactly two successes have probability
(42)(1/4)2(3/4)2=27/128

, option 4. 3. An independent derivation conditions on the number K of first-round heads. Sum (4k)2-4(k2)2-k for k=2,3,4. The contributions are 3/32,3/32,3/128, whose sum is 27/128. 4. Treating the second round as four unconditional fair tosses ignores that only first-round heads qualify. Fixing the random number of qualifying coins at its expected value also changes the distribution.

Transfer rule. Replace a multistage selection experiment by independent per-object indicators when eligibility and success can be combined into one event.

Positive allocations with a lower-bound shift

Question 16. Positive allocations with a lower-bound shift — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q113; MS_CS_1405_Q115. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Count positive integer triples with sum n+3. Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

1.
15
2.
64
3.
21
4.
28
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

Step 1 — model and conditions. Subtract one from each positive variable, leaving a nonnegative total of n across three variables. Two separators among n+2 positions describe all allocations uniquely. The lower bounds reduce the total before separator counting.

Step 2 — compute. The general expression is (n+22). Substituting n=5 gives 21. Keep the exact value until all constraints have been applied.

Step 3 — audit the alternatives. The other listed values are 28, 15, 64. They are obtained from the three competing expressions (n+32), (n+12), (n+3)2, respectively. Those expressions discard or alter a condition in the model; the derivation above shows where the discrepancy enters. Recomputing the defining constraints, rather than selecting the numerically nearest option, determines the answer.

Concept model supporting this solution

Question 18. Positive allocations with a lower-bound shift — symbolic generalization

Derive before generalizing. Subtract one from each positive variable, leaving a nonnegative total of n across three variables. Two separators among n+2 positions describe all allocations uniquely. The lower bounds reduce the total before separator counting. Therefore the expression is (n+22). The three alternatives (n+32), (n+12), (n+3)2 violate the counting, algebraic or model conditions identified in that derivation. The exact instances above are useful checks, but agreement at one special parameter does not establish a general identity. Question 19. Positive allocations with a lower-bound shift — applicability and boundary

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q113; MS_CS_1405_Q115. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Count positive integer triples with sum n+3. Which statement correctly identifies the scope or a failure of this method?

1.

Positive and nonnegative allocations have identical counts.

2.

A negative residual total still has stars-and-bars solutions.

3.

Ordering the allocated units multiplies the count by a factorial.

4.

Different lower bounds require subtracting their sum before counting.

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 4.

Check the hypothesis. A shift is a bijection between the constrained allocation and a nonnegative residual allocation. It is feasible only when the residual total is nonnegative. Units are indistinguishable in integer allocation, while the variable identities remain labeled.

Connect it to the calculation. Subtract one from each positive variable, leaving a nonnegative total of n across three variables. Two separators among n+2 positions describe all allocations uniquely. The lower bounds reduce the total before separator counting. The valid statement is: Different lower bounds require subtracting their sum before counting. A formula can remain numerically correct in one exceptional case after its assumptions are removed, but that does not justify using it as a general rule. Distinguish the mathematical identity from the modeling assumptions that permit this identity to count or measure the requested objects.

Concept model supporting this solution

Step 1 — model and conditions. Partition the event by the exact red count: three, four or five. The cases are disjoint and their blue counts are respectively two, one and zero. Multiply within each case and add across cases; a chosen qualifying triple would overcount larger red selections.

. Substituting n=5 gives 126. Keep the exact value until all constraints have been applied.

Step 1 — model and conditions. Use inclusion-exclusion on the event that each specified position is fixed. Fixing a chosen set of j positions leaves (n-j)! permutations. Multiplying by the choice of that set simplifies each alternating term to n!/j!.

Step 3 — audit the alternatives. The other listed values are 20922789888000, 40320, 1290240. They are obtained from the three competing expressions (2n)!, n!, 2n(n-1)!, respectively. Those expressions discard or alter a condition in the model; the derivation above shows where the discrepancy enters. Recomputing the defining constraints, rather than selecting the numerically nearest option, determines the answer.

Question 66. Collapsing blocks without losing internal order — symbolic generalization

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q113; MS_CS_1405_Q115. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Arrange n distinct couples in a line of 2n seats, requiring each couple to sit together. Count arrangements. Which general expression gives the requested quantity for all parameters in the positive-integer parameter domain, subject to the additional conditions stated above?

1.
n!
2.
2n(n-1)!
3.
2nn!
4.
(2n)!
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

Derive before generalizing. Collapse each couple into a distinct block. The blocks can be ordered in n! ways, and each has two internal orientations. Multiplying these independent choices preserves both block identity and the distinguishable people inside each block. Therefore the expression is 2nn!. The three alternatives (2n)!, n!, 2n(n-1)! violate the counting, algebraic or model conditions identified in that derivation. The exact instances above are useful checks, but agreement at one special parameter does not establish a general identity. The quantifier in this question requires validity over the entire specified parameter domain.

Question 67. Collapsing blocks without losing internal order — applicability and boundary

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q113; MS_CS_1405_Q115. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Arrange n distinct couples in a line of 2n seats, requiring each couple to sit together. Count arrangements. Which statement correctly identifies the scope or a failure of this method?

1.

All couples become indistinguishable after collapsing.

2.

A circular-seating version requires a different block-order factor.

3.

Collapsing a block removes all internal orientations.

4.

The line and circle have the same rotation convention.

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

Check the hypothesis. The block trick simplifies adjacency but does not erase member labels. On a circle, rotational equivalence changes the arrangement factor for blocks. In a line there is a distinguished left-to-right order and rotations are not identified.

Connect it to the calculation. Collapse each couple into a distinct block. The blocks can be ordered in n! ways, and each has two internal orientations. Multiplying these independent choices preserves both block identity and the distinguishable people inside each block. The valid statement is: A circular-seating version requires a different block-order factor. A formula can remain numerically correct in one exceptional case after its assumptions are removed, but that does not justify using it as a general rule. Distinguish the mathematical identity from the modeling assumptions that permit this identity to count or measure the requested objects.

Question 68. Integer solutions with parity and two bounds

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q129. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Count nonnegative integer solutions of a+b+c=18 with a even, b≤3, and c≥2.

1.

32

2.

33

3.

34

4.

36

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

Set a=2j and c=c'+2. Then 2j+b+c'=16. For b=0,1,2,3, the numbers of allowed j are 9,8,8,7, respectively.

Each determines exactly one c', so add to obtain 32. The even endpoint at sixteen makes the four cases unequal. Ordinary stars and bars ignores parity and the upper bound; dividing an unrestricted count by two is unjustified at a finite boundary.

Question 69. An onto map with a fiber lower bound

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q124. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Count surjections from a five-element labeled set to three labeled outputs when the first output has at least two preimages.

1.

80

2.

100

3.

120

4.

150

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

The distinguished fiber has size two or three; larger sizes leave too few inputs to hit both remaining outputs. At size two, choose the fiber in ten ways and use one of six onto maps from the remaining three inputs to two outputs, giving sixty.

At size three, choose the fiber in ten ways and biject the other two inputs in two ways, giving twenty. The total is eighty. One hundred includes a missing-output case; 150 counts every surjection without the fiber restriction. Fiber-size cases are disjoint, so their counts must be added.

2.

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

The even zero counts are zero, two, and four, giving

25+(52)23+(54)2=32+80+10=122

.

Equivalently the parity filter is (35+15)/2. The total 243 is odd, so the parity classes cannot have exactly equal sizes. One hundred twenty-one is the odd-zero class; eighty-one counts a different fixed-length unrestricted alphabet.

Question 74. Equal head counts by Vandermonde

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1404_Q70. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Two independent fair-coin experiments have eight and five tosses. What is the probability of equal head counts?

1.
(135)/213
2.
(138)/28
3.
(85)/213
4.
1/2
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

Sum over the common head count: 2-13∑k=05(8k)(5k). Replace the second coefficient by (55-k); Vandermonde gives (135).

All thirteen tosses contribute to the denominator. The combination (85) omits possible successes in the second experiment. Complementing the second experiment's heads gives an equivalent single-binomial event, but does not imply probability one half.

Question 76. Lower and upper bounds together

Original integrated challenge · retained after review

How many integer solutions satisfy x1+x2+x3+x4=12 with 1≤xi≤5?

1. 65

2. 80

3. 85

4. 165

Correct option: 3.

Shift yi=xi-1 to nonnegative variables summing to8 with upper bound4. Unrestricted count is (113)=165. A violation yi≥5 leaves sum3 and count (63)=20; there are four possible violating variables. Two violations need sum at least10 and are impossible. Thus165-4(20)=85. Applying upper-bound exclusion before accounting for the lower-bound shift can use the wrong forbidden threshold.

Question 77. Uniform sequences versus multisets

Original integrated challenge · retained after review

Three independent fair binary digits are sampled. What is the probability that the induced multiset contains two zeros and one one?

1. 1/4

2. 3/8

3. 1/2

4. 2/3

Correct option: 2.

There are eight equally likely ordered strings. The desired multiset has three realizations:001,010,100, so probability is3/8. The four possible multisets are not uniformly distributed: the all-zero and all-one multisets each have one realization, while the two mixed multisets each have three. Dividing by the number of multisets therefore changes the sampling law.

Applicable formulas and examination notes

1. Order and replacement

Ordered distinct samples use n!/(n-r)!; unordered distinct samples use (nr); ordered repeated selections use nr. For 7 objects and 3 distinct picks, these first two counts are 210 and 35. State the counted object before selecting a formula.

2. Identical copies

Fixed multiplicities n1,…,nk among N positions give N!/∏ni!. BANANA gives 6!/(3!2!)=60. Divide by the factorial of each multiplicity, not merely by the number of repeated letters.

3. Positive versus nonnegative

For positive k variables summing to N, subtract 1 from every variable and use (N-1k-1). Nonnegative variables use (N+k-1k-1). Inconsistent lower bounds give zero rather than a negative factorial.

4. Upper-bound shift

For xi≤b, a bad variable begins at b+1. Shift by b+1 in inclusion-exclusion. For three variables summing to7 with bound 3, unrestricted 36 minus three bad counts of10 gives 6; two bad variables are impossible.

5. Surjections

Onto maps from n labeled objects to k labeled boxes number ∑j=0k(-1)j(kj)(k-j)n. For n=4,k=3, the answer is36. Missing a box is an event, and missing-box events overlap.

6. Unlabeled boxes

For exactly k nonempty groups of labeled objects, divide the onto count by k!. All groups being nonempty ensures each partition has exactly k! labelings. Allowing empty boxes introduces stabilizers and invalidates a blind division.

7. Isolated positions

Binary strings with r nonadjacent ones have (n-r+1r) arrangements. There are n-r+1 gaps among the zeros. Select distinct gaps; allowing several ones in one gap violates isolation.

8. Uniform committees

For r selected from groups of sizes a,b, exactly j from the first group has count (aj)(br-j) out of (a+br). The ratio is justified by uniform sampling of subsets, not by an unstated independent model.

9. Adjacency blocks

Two specified distinct objects adjacent in n permutations have 2(n-1)! favorable orders, probability 2/n. If their order is fixed, remove the factor 2. A chain of overlapping adjacency constraints may not behave like independent blocks.

10. Circular symmetry

Distinct objects modulo rotation give (n-1)! orders. Keeping versus identifying reflections is a separate convention. With repeated symbols, rotational orbits can have different sizes, so dividing every linear count by n can fail.

11. Pigeonhole threshold

To force at least r objects in one of k boxes, the sharp unrestricted threshold is k(r-1)+1. Construct the balanced counterexample with r-1 per box to prove that one fewer is insufficient.

12. Multisets are not uniform sequence outcomes

Multisets of size r from k types number (k+r-1r). A multiset with counts ni has r!/∏ni! sequence realizations. Different multiplicities yield different induced probabilities when sequences are drawn uniformly.

13. Vandermonde decomposition

∑j(aj)(br-j)=(a+br) partitions all r -subsets by their first-group count. Terms with inadmissible indices are zero. Restricting the summation to a smaller range counts an additional constraint, not the full identity.

14. Weighted subset counts

∑j=0nj(nj)=n2n-1 counts a subset with one distinguished included element. A second distinct ordered distinguished element gives ∑j(j-1)(nj)=n(n-1)2n-2. Replacing j(j-1) by j2 requires adding the one-element term.

15. Collision probability complement

For r independent uniform choices from n types, no collision has probability n!/[(n-r)!nr] when r≤n. Collision probability is one minus that value. Independence of choices does not mean the pairwise collision events are independent.

11. References and source-use record

Core reviewed courses

  1. Massachusetts Institute of Technology — John N. Tsitsiklis. 6.041/6.431 Probabilistic Systems Analysis and Applied Probability, Fall 2010. Lecture 3: Independence, instructional pages 1–2; Lecture 4: Counting, instructional pages 1–2. Used for the counting-to-probability contract, selection models, partitions, the product definition, complement independence, and hidden-mixture examples. The attribution page is separate from the instructional scope.
  2. Stanford University — Lisa Yan; foundational notes credited to Mehran Sahami and Chris Piech where stated. CS109: Probability for Computer Scientists, Spring 2020. Lecture Notes 01: Counting, pages 1–4; Lecture Notes 02: Combinatorics, pages 1–7; Lecture Notes 05: Independence, pages 1–5. Used for staged counting, stars and bars, occupancy, binomial pattern weights, repeated races, and conditional selection. The source's final geometric-series sentence on Lecture Notes 05 page 3 has an indexing slip; Section 6.6 derives the corrected series explicitly. This chapter uses probability mass, rather than the source's occasional density wording for a binomial law.
  3. University of California, Berkeley — CS70 course staff. Discrete Mathematics and Probability Theory, Summer 2019; course instructors James Hulett and Elizabeth Yang. Official course archive; Note 12: Counting, pages 1–5; Note 12.5: Other Counting Techniques and Combinatorial Proofs, pages 1–4; Note 14: Conditional Probability, independence section on pages 6–11. Used for equal-fiber proofs, occupancy versus placements, combinatorial identities, independence subfamilies, pattern equivalence, and conditional-law distinctions. The PDF notes do not individually name an author; the instructors are identified as instructors, not asserted to be their individual authors.
  4. University of Oxford — Elias Koutsoupias. Probability and Computing, 2016–2017. Course and instructor; official written lectures, Lecture 2 independence definitions and Lecture 18 pairwise independence and “Bits for free.” Used for the distinction between pairwise and mutual independence and the computational parity perspective. The chapter's continuous parity family and its proof are original extensions; no claim is made to have reviewed unrelated lectures in full.

Selection and attribution limits

The accompanying source audit records a bounded candidate survey, selection reasons, accessible written sections, and excluded or inaccessible candidates. Four universities contribute genuinely reviewed instructional material. This is not a claim that every course worldwide has been inspected or that exactly four sources will suffice for every later chapter.

The lesson is an original synthesis, with original proofs, figures, finite models, and worked problem formulations. Related university examples are used to choose and cross-check teaching methods; this chapter does not reproduce the courses' complete copyrighted exercise banks. Accordingly, its problem bank is explicitly identified as original, and the linked courses remain the primary locations for their own complete materials. All references and explanatory source notes are in English.
